questions.prompt: A prompted model answers customers politely and in the right format, but quotes a renewal fee that was correct last year. Which change addresses the cause?
options: Fine-tune it on this year's conversations
Give it the current fee table in the context
Lower the sampling temperature
Distil a larger model's answers into it
questions.explanation: The fee is a fact that changes; a fact belongs in the context, where it can be updated and dated.
misconceptions: Puts a changing fact into weights, where it will be wrong again next year
Treats a wrong fact as randomness in generation
Copies the larger model's behaviour, which does not contain this year's fee either

questions.prompt: On 100 requests a small model makes 30 behaviour failures and a larger model, with the same instructions, makes 4. What does the pair of counts support?
options: The behaviour can be taught to the small model, by tuning or distillation
The requests are too hard for any model
The small model lacks a fact that must be retrieved
The grading code is wrong for the small model
questions.explanation: The larger model shows that the right behaviour exists for these requests; the gap is what tuning or distillation can aim at.
misconceptions: Ignores that the larger model handles the same requests
Confuses a wrong decision with a missing fact: a missing fact would fail on both models
Blames the instrument without evidence: both models were graded by the same code

questions.prompt: A model's answer is the correct tool call, written inside a Markdown code fence instead of the required tags, and the parser rejects it. Which failure class is it?
options: Not a failure, because the decision is right
Knowledge
Behaviour
Format
questions.explanation: The decision is right and its wrapping is wrong: a schema hint, an example or tuning on the format fixes it.
misconceptions: Forgets that the registry only accepts what parses
Sees a rejected call and assumes a missing fact
Calls every wrong answer a wrong decision, although the tool and arguments are right

questions.prompt: Which task is the best candidate for a tuned small model on one accelerator?
options: Planning a company's tax filing across several systems
Answering any question about commercial law
Extracting the same eight fields from thousands of similar forms
Reviewing rare contracts that each need a lawyer's judgement
questions.explanation: One input, one structured output that a program can check, at volume: the narrow shape a small tuned model suits.
misconceptions: Chooses multi-step work that depends on intermediate results
Chooses an open-ended knowledge task, which tuning teaches badly
Chooses rare inputs that each need judgement nobody can label at volume

questions.prompt: A team reports that fine-tuning raised accuracy from 31% to 82%. The 31% used a one-sentence prompt. What should a reviewer ask for first?
options: A comparison with a model twice the size
The score of the best prompt they could write on the same model
A larger training set
The training loss curve
questions.explanation: Until the untuned model has been given a strong prompt, nobody knows how much of the gain needed training.
misconceptions: Changes the question from "did tuning help this model" to "which model is bigger"
Asks for more of the thing whose effect is not yet established
Checks that training ran, not what it should be compared with

questions.prompt: Two prompt versions score 50 and 52 right out of the same 100 requests. Which statement is supported?
options: The versions cannot be told apart on this evidence
Version two would score 52% on any hundred requests
One hundred requests prove nothing about either
Version two is better by two points
questions.explanation: A difference of two requests in 100 is far inside the sampling noise of each score.
misconceptions: Treats a sample score as a property of the model
Throws away a measurement that does bound each score to about ten points either way
Reads a difference without asking how large the noise is

questions.prompt: After the baseline was frozen, an engineer improves one sentence of the instructions and keeps quoting the old score. What is wrong?
options: The set must be changed as well
The score should be averaged with the new one
Nothing: one sentence cannot change a score
The old score belongs to a text that is no longer used; the new text must be scored and frozen again
questions.explanation: A baseline is a text, a set and a score together; when the text changes, the pairing is broken.
misconceptions: Changes the second fixed element too, losing every earlier comparison
Mixes two different systems into one number
Assumes small edits have no effect, which is exactly what scoring is for

questions.prompt: A licence allows anyone to fine-tune a model for research, and allows use in a product only under a separate agreement. A company fine-tunes it and now wants to put it in its paid service. What is its position?
options: It may: the fine-tuned model is its own work
It may: research use includes testing in production
It may not without the separate agreement: adapting was licensed, this deployment is not
It may, if it does not distribute the weights
questions.explanation: Adapting and deploying are separate permissions; the adapted model is a derivative under the same terms.
misconceptions: Believes tuning creates a new work free of the original licence
Stretches "research" to cover a paid service
Mixes up distribution with commercial use: not sharing the weights does not license the use

questions.prompt: A model card shows the licence tag "other". What is the next step before choosing the model?
options: Assume it is permissive, since the weights are public
Open the licence file in the repository, read it and record the date
Ask in a forum what "other" usually means
Train first and check the licence before deployment
questions.explanation: The tag is a label; the file is the licence, and it can change with a later release.
misconceptions: Reads availability as permission
Replaces the text with someone's opinion of it
Spends the training budget before knowing whether the result can be used

questions.prompt: A licence grants commercial use only to organisations under a revenue threshold. Which pair of facts must the licence table record for an organisation that wants to deploy?
options: Its annual revenue and whether the intended use is commercial under the licence's definition
The model's size and its benchmark scores
The size of the fine-tuning set and the number of adapters
Its number of employees and its country
questions.explanation: The clause turns on revenue against the threshold and on the purpose of the use; both are facts about the organisation.
misconceptions: Describes the model, not the licensee
Describes the project, which the clause does not depend on
Records facts the clause does not mention

questions.prompt: An owned accelerator costs SAR 6,000 a month in total and serves 30,000 requests a month. What is the cost per thousand requests?
options: SAR 180
SAR 2
SAR 20
SAR 200
questions.explanation: 6,000 divided by 30 thousands of requests is SAR 200 per thousand.
misconceptions: Multiplies the monthly cost by the volume in tens of thousands instead of dividing
Divides by 3,000 thousands: a slip of two decimal places
Divides by 300 thousands: a slip of one decimal place

questions.prompt: A hosted model costs SAR 0.50 per thousand requests and a tuned small model on the organisation's own servers costs SAR 140. The requests are classified Restricted and must stay on the organisation's servers. What should the decision memo say?
options: The small model is the cheaper option
The hosted model is chosen, because cost decides
The small model is chosen for placement, at a stated premium per thousand requests
Cost cannot be compared, because the options are different
questions.explanation: The requirement rules the hosted option out; the memo states the premium honestly and why it is paid.
misconceptions: States the opposite of the measured numbers
Ignores a requirement that the cheaper option does not meet
Avoids a comparison that the same unit makes possible

questions.prompt: A prompted request carries 600 tokens of instructions and examples and 30 tokens of request. After tuning, the instructions are no longer sent. What happens to the input cost per request on a per-token price?
options: It falls by 30 tokens
It falls to about a twentieth
It stays the same, because the output is unchanged
It doubles, because adapters add tokens
questions.explanation: Input falls from about 630 tokens to about 30: the tuned model reads only the request.
misconceptions: Subtracts the request instead of the instructions
Confuses input and output tokens
Believes an adapter adds tokens: it adds weights, not text

questions.prompt: A tuning set is built only from traces that staff accepted without change. What is the model most likely to learn from it?
options: To repeat what it already does
To fix the failures staff corrected most often
To handle the hardest requests, which staff reviewed with most care
Nothing, because accepted traces carry no label
questions.explanation: An accepted trace is labelled by the model's own output, so the set repeats current behaviour.
misconceptions: Expects corrections to be present in a set that left them out
Assumes acceptance means careful review; the hardest requests are the ones staff abandoned or corrected
Forgets that the accepted output is itself the label

questions.prompt: A staff correction gives a registration number of nine digits; the tool requires ten. The intended number can be guessed from the request. What is the sound handling?
options: Use the model's original answer as the label instead
Add the missing digit and keep the row as a staff correction
Keep the row as typed, because staff labels outrank the schema
Drop the row and report it in the counts
questions.explanation: The tool would refuse the call, so it is not a usable label; dropping it visibly keeps every label traceable to its source.
misconceptions: Uses the answer that staff rejected as a training target
Enters the engineer's guess under the desk's name, with no record of the change
Trains the model to produce a call the tool refuses

questions.prompt: A verifier keeps 97% of a teacher model's labels. A colleague writes "label accuracy: 97%" in the dataset card. What is wrong with the sentence?
options: A card should not contain numbers that can change
Nothing: the verifier measured it
Yield counts what passed the checks, not what is right
The figure should be 3%, the share rejected
questions.explanation: Passing schema and rule checks shows a label is well-formed and consistent with its request; whether it is right needs an audit.
misconceptions: Removes the evidence a reader needs instead of correcting it
Treats passing a check as being correct
Reports the rejected share as if it were the error rate of what was kept

questions.prompt: A request names two registration numbers: the applicant's and a partner's. The teacher's call uses the partner's. Which check catches the error?
options: A rule that the number in the call must appear in the request
An audit by a person who reads the request
A check that the call parses as JSON
The schema check, because the number is invalid
questions.explanation: The call is valid and its number is in the request; only someone who makes the decision again can see that it is the wrong number.
misconceptions: Overlooks that the partner's number does appear in the request
Checks the form of a call whose form is fine
Assumes a wrong number is a malformed one: it has ten digits and passes

questions.prompt: Staff audit 30 kept teacher labels and find no error. Which statement belongs in the dataset card?
options: No error in an audit of 30, which allows a true rate of up to about 11%
The audit was too small to report
The kept labels contain no errors
The error rate of the kept labels is below 1%
questions.explanation: Zero in 30 bounds the rate; it does not show it is zero. The 95% upper bound is about 11%.
misconceptions: Hides a measurement that, with its bound, is useful to the reader
Reads "none found" as "none exist"
States a precision that a sample of 30 cannot give

questions.prompt: After tuning, a model writes the correct tool call and then continues generating until the token limit. The training loss fell normally. What is the most likely cause?
options: The learning rate was too low
The adapter rank was too small to learn stopping
The tuning set held too few examples
The training text had no end-of-turn token after the answer
questions.explanation: A model stops because it was shown stopping; if the rendered text never closes the turn, no setting teaches it to.
misconceptions: Looks for an optimisation fault although the loss behaved normally
Treats a missing token in the data as a capacity limit
Blames quantity for a fault every example shares

questions.prompt: In a tuning example the user's request is 26 tokens and the assistant's answer 56. With a correct label mask, on how many tokens is the loss taken?
questions.explanation: The prompt is masked with the ignore index; the loss is taken on the assistant's turn only.
misconceptions: Subtracts the two counts instead of masking one of them
Supervises the request and ignores the answer: the mask reversed
Takes the loss on the whole conversation, which trains the model to predict requests

questions.prompt: A team renders its tuning set with a hand-written format and serves the adapter behind a server that applies the base model's chat template. What should they expect?
options: No effect, because the words are the same
Lower quality in service than in their own evaluation
Slower training only
An error when the adapter loads
questions.explanation: The adapter learnt one string format and is sent another; their own evaluation used the hand-written format and hides the gap.
misconceptions: Ignores that role markers and special tokens are part of what the model reads
Expects a cost in speed where the cost is in what was learnt
Expects a loud failure: a format mismatch raises no error

questions.prompt: A tuning row nearly copies a test request and names the same company registration number. How is it handled?
options: Removed from the tuning set and counted as a leak
Kept, and the test request is deleted instead
Kept, because the label may differ
Kept, because near-copies are not exact copies
questions.explanation: It is a test case inside the training data: every later score would be too high by an unknown amount.
misconceptions: Changes the test set after results exist, which breaks earlier comparisons
Looks at the label although the leak is in the request the model is examined on
Applies an exact-match standard that a greeting defeats

questions.prompt: A near-duplicate rule at a lower threshold removes 82 rows; at a higher one, 67. What should decide between them?
options: The threshold used in a published paper
The lower threshold, because a smaller set trains faster
The higher threshold, because more data is always better
Reading a sample of the pairs each one removes
questions.explanation: A threshold is right when what it removes are duplicates; only reading the removed pairs shows whether different requests were merged.
misconceptions: Borrows a number tuned on other data, with other text lengths
Chooses by training time, not by whether the removed rows were duplicates
Keeps rows without asking whether they are repeats

questions.prompt: After masking, a scan for phone numbers, identity numbers, e-mail addresses and names from the member registry finds nothing. Which claim can the dataset card make?
options: The set may be published
The set contains no personal data
The scan found none of four kinds, with names taken from one list
Personal data was removed in line with the law, so no further review is needed
questions.explanation: A scan reports on what it looks for: a name outside the list, or a kind it does not know, passes.
misconceptions: Draws a release decision from a scan that covers four kinds
Turns "none found by this scan" into "none exists"
Turns one technical step into a legal conclusion

questions.prompt: Personal data is masked in the tuning set with placeholders such as [PHONE]. In service, requests reach the model unmasked. What is the main consequence?
options: None: the model ignores digits
The model meets inputs unlike its training data, and its logs hold personal data
Training must be repeated with a larger rank
The adapter no longer loads on the base model
questions.explanation: The same masking function must run in front of the model in service, so that training and service inputs match.
misconceptions: Assumes a tuned model is indifferent to tokens it never saw in that position
Answers a data mismatch with a capacity setting
Expects a loading error from a difference in input text
